questions.question: A team computes the distance from brake release to main-wheel liftoff and reports it as the total takeoff distance of MIL-STD-3013. What is missing?
options: The air distance from liftoff to clear 50 ft
The distance to stop after an engine failure
The rotation distance before main-wheel liftoff
A correction for headwind and runway slope
questions.explanation: Brake release to main-wheel liftoff is the ground run. The total takeoff distance adds the air distance to clear 50 ft; the stop after an engine failure belongs to the critical field length.

questions.question: A trailing-edge flap is deflected on a clean airfoil. What happens to the section lift curve?
options: It shifts up and to the left: Clmax rises and αstall falls
It extends along the same line: Clmax and αstall both rise
It shifts up and to the right: Clmax and αstall both rise
It gets steeper: Clmax rises and αstall stays the same
questions.explanation: The flap shifts the curve up and to the left, so the higher Clmax comes at a lower αstall. Extending the curve to a higher αstall is the effect of a slot or slat.

questions.question: What gives the Fowler flap the largest section increment ΔClmax of the trailing-edge devices?
options: It moves aft, adding chord as well as camber
It opens two slots that keep the flow attached
It deflects to a larger angle than the others
It leaves the upper surface of the wing unchanged
questions.explanation: The Fowler flap moves well back before it deflects, so it adds chord and camber. The cost is tracks and a nose-down pitching moment.

questions.question: A table of typical values gives CLmax/cos Λ = 2.0 for a high-lift system. Which CLmax does that imply for an invented wing with 30° of sweep?
questions.explanation: CLmax = 2.0 × cos 30° = 1.73. The table lists CLmax over the cosine of the wing sweep, so a swept wing reaches less than the listed number.

questions.question: In the wing partition method, which lift coefficient does an unflapped segment carry in the sum?
options: The clean section Cl at the flapped section's αstall
The clean section Clmax at the clean section's αstall
The flapped section Clmax with the device increment
The clean section Clmax times cos Λhinge
questions.explanation: The flapped section stalls at a lower α than the clean section, so the unflapped segments are taken at that angle. In the SR22 example that is Cl = 1.562 at 12°, below the clean Clmax of 1.62 at 16°.

questions.question: A slat lets an aircraft fly the FCLP approach at a lower speed. What does that do to the approach angle of attack α<sub>pa</sub> and to the view the pilot needs over the nose?
options: α<sub>pa</sub> rises, and the view over the nose must cover a larger angle
α<sub>pa</sub> falls, and the view over the nose can cover a smaller angle
α<sub>pa</sub> rises, and the view over the nose depends on the glide slope only
α<sub>pa</sub> stays the same, and only the glide slope becomes steeper
questions.explanation: Flying slower on a slat raises α<sub>pa</sub>, and the view over the nose must cover α<sub>pa</sub> plus the angle from the flight path down to the stern. Flaps do the opposite: they lower α<sub>pa</sub>.

questions.question: Why is takeoff flown with partial flap deflection and landing with full deflection?
options: Takeoff needs L/D to climb; landing uses drag for a steeper approach
Takeoff is at a lower weight than landing; landing needs the extra lift
Takeoff needs the highest CLmax; landing needs the lowest drag
Takeoff flaps separate above 15° of deflection; landing flaps do not
questions.explanation: Flap drag grows with deflection. Takeoff keeps the deflection partial to hold the climb L/D. Landing uses full deflection: it gives the highest CLmax, and the drag steepens the approach.

questions.question: Why is the lift dumped during the braking roll?
options: Lift unloads the wheels and cuts the braking force
Lift adds drag, and drag lengthens the braking roll
Lift raises the stall speed and with it the touchdown speed
Lift raises the flare height and lengthens the flare
questions.explanation: The braking force is μ(W − L), so lift on the wing takes weight off the wheels and lengthens SBR. Drag acts with the brakes and shortens the roll.
